html:
The Dancing Girl is a small bronze figure of a young woman, about 10.5 cm tall, found at Mohenjo-daro, a city of the Indus Valley civilisation in today's Pakistan. It was made about 2300 to 1750 BCE.

It was cast by the lost-wax method: a wax model is covered in clay, the wax melted out, and metal poured in. That makes it one of the earliest known bronze castings of a human figure in South Asia.

She stands naked in a relaxed, confident pose, one hand on her hip. Her left arm is covered almost to the shoulder in bangles, and she wears a necklace; her hair is gathered in a bun. She was found in 1926. Nobody knows if she was a dancer; the name is a modern guess.

After the partition of India in 1947, India kept her and she is in the National Museum in New Delhi; Pakistan has asked for her return. Compare the sealing art of the Indus script.
